newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FORECAST - SIA seen maintaining earnings.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - SIA seen maintaining earnings.

text.p: Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) is widely expected to maintain its earnings at above one billion dollars despite a year made difficult by high fuel prices and a weaker yen, analysts said on Wednesday.

Analysts polled in The Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimate Directory gave a concensus forecast of Singapore $1.04 billion (US$722 million) in 1997 net earnings for the airline, fractionally higher than 1996's S$1.03 billion.
Of the 33 analysts polled, the lowest forecast was S$931.2 million and the highest was S$1.09 billion.
SIA is expected to announce its results for the 1997 financial year ended March 31 on May 16.
"SIA had a tough FY1997 but I expect it would still be able to breach the one billion dollar mark," said Nora Cheng, associate director of research with HSBC James Capel.
Cheng, who has forecast SIA net profits at around S$1.04, said she expected core airline operations to be weak but earnings to be cushioned by aircraft sales and profits from other businesses.
Analysts said SIA had about eight aircraft for sale and the market for second hand aircraft had picked up.
But most of the aircraft sales would probably be in the 1998 financial year, they said.

Declan Magee, regional airline analyst with ABN-AMBRO Hoare Govett Securities, said that while SIA's passenger traffic had picked up, its bottom line had been affected by stiff competition and a weak Japanese yen.
"Passenger trafffic has done very well. But average ticket prices have been affected by competition," he said.
A weak yen against the Singapore dollar would also affect passenger yields as Japan is a major market for SIA, he said.

Magee, who has forecast a 1997 net profit of S$1.05 billion, said that while fuel prices had been falling since the start of the year, SIA's 1997 fuel bill would still on average be much higher than in the previous year.
Lee Kin Wah, research manager with Jardine Fleming International Securities, said some SIA subsidiaries could surprise on the upside.
"The surprise could come from SilkAir which may become profitable and SIA Engineering should also do well judging from the results at ST Aerospace," Lee said.
However, any gains in these subsidiaries would have a limited impact as the core airline business contributes up to 80 percent of profits, he said.
The analysts said they expected SIA's 1998 earnings to be better because of more aircraft sales and lower fuel costs.
Some also said they expected the Japanese yen to firm from its current weakness, especially in the later part of 1998.

SIA's foreign share price has been gaining in recent weeks on such rosy prospects but analysts also attribute the gains to market speculation that the company may be giving out a special bonus dividend to celebrate its 50th anniversary this year.
